Work Culture of CPWD 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the MINISTER OF URBAN 
PMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
nether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item i "A 
case of shocking apathy", which appeared in the Hindu, (Delhi), '30th 
September, 2001; 
so, the details in this regard; 
action taken against the guilty officers of CPWD; and 
 fresh steps taken/proposed to be taken by Government to improve 
culture of CPWD? 
MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
IATION (SHRI ANANTH KUMAR): (a) to (d)A Statement is laid on the 
abha. 
(d) An enquiry conducted in the matter revealed that there was a 
jetween the allottee of Quarter No. D-681, Netaji Nagar, New Delhi and 
orkers of the contractor engaged by the CPWD on 31st July, 2001, ig 
which the labour left the Quarter without completing the work ng to 
electrical rewiring. This complaint was brought to the notice of 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
CPWD on 7th August, 2001 and an Assistance Engineer visited the premises on 
the same date and got the electricity re stored. The allottee, in his statement 
before the Enquiry Officer, has confirmed that he has no complaint against the 
CPWD staff, who were helpful and co operative and it was the contractor's 
workers who were abusive. As there is no lapse on the part of CPWD Officers, 
no action against them is warranted. Howe ver, the workers of the contractor 
involved in the quarrel with the allottee were removed from work by the contractor. 
The Officers and workers of CPWD are constantly being oriented and trained 
to further improve their inter-personal relations with the allottees. An Interactive 
voice Response System has also recently been introduced in two service centres 
in Delhi. 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Hon. Chairman, Sir, this is a very 
important question which relates to the maintenance of CPWD quarters, which 
includes quarters of all dignitaries, bur eaucrats, Government employees, etc. 
Sir, the question relates to a news item which appeared in "The Hindu." But the 
hon. Minister has given a general reply. Sir, what has been said is that that was 
a mistake on the part of the contract labour. So, much importance has not been 
given to the incident, and the contractor  has just axed the contract labour 
involved in the incident. Sir, the question here is not whether the CPWD quarters 
will be repaired by the contractor or by the CPWD. That is a different thing. But 
the question here is one of maintenan ce of the CPWD quarters which is the 
responsibility of the CPWD. Sir, it has been seen that the maintenance of the 
CPWD quarters in Delhi is very poor, irrespective of the fact whether it is a 
quarter of a Member of Parliament or  of a bureaucrat or of a Government 
employee. The first point is, the complaints are not being attended to at all. 
The second point, is, whether the contractor conducts any inquiry before 
engaging the contract labour, which has been sent to the quarter for attending 
to the complaint, with regard to his identity, etc. I would like to know whether 
the Government has got any information as to whom the contractor is engaging 
as contract labour. Someti mes, there is a complaint that the contract labour 
which is sent to attend to the complaint is involved in theft cases or in certain 
serious cases. May be, they are involved in such cases. So, I would like to know 
whether there are any particular guidelines which the contractor has to follow 
while employing labour. The contractor has to enquire about the Contract 
labour in order to avoid the unwarranted incidents. 
My third point is related to CPWD itself. I would like to know whether the 
CPWD has got any particular statistics as to how many Governments quarters 
2 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
in Delhi are in a bad shape and in a dilapidated condition, i.e., are not in a 
habitable condition. Although there are a lot of complaints, the CPWD is not 
taking appropriate action. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, regarding the point relating to grievances, 
there is a mechanism. It is a three-fold mechanism. One is, we have got 103 
centres in Delhi, which service the grievances of the occupants. Each service 
centre is being manned by a junior engineer, and Sir, in important places, where 
the houses are larger in number, even an Assistant Engineer is available. 
Secondly, Sir, about 15 days back, we have launched a system called IVRS, 
i.e., Interactive Voice Response System in two of the centres so that the grievances, 
the complaints, could be monitored on a real-time basis. Thirdly, in Ghaziabad, 
we have got an institution to give refresher courses, especially, in inter-personal 
relationship as well as in client satisfaction. Sir, it is an on-going process; that 
also is being done. Now, Sir, there are three types of complaints. One is, essential 
types of complaints like water connection, electricity, etc. which will be attended 
to in less than 24 hours. The second one is the routine type of complaints, like 
tower bolts, flooring, which need three days' time. The third ones—I don't call 
them as complaints—are known as request s for additions and alterations. They 
are processed in a week or fifteen days' time. There is a mechanism for these. But, 
having said this, I do not say that everything is hunky-dory. We need to improve 
our services. There is a lot of scope for improvement. 
In the aforesaid case, the CPWD does all its maintenance work through the 
contracting agencies. As soon as the incident took place, the three workers, 
who were on contract, were removed by the contractor. It is very difficult to 
trace them out since we do not know where they have gone. But, Sir, even the 
occupants, the house-owner, has given a statement stating that the CPWD Junior 
Engineer, Assistant Engineer, Executive Engineer were very cooperative and 
they have behaved very well. 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTI A: Sir, if the hon. Minister says that these 
are properly maintained, I would like to know the number of complaints that have 
been received by the CPWD during th e month of November, and how many 
complaints have been attended to. 
Sir, the point made by me has not been answered by the hon. Minister. Sir, it 
is not a question of a single worker. It is a question of attitude of the CPWD for 
the maintenance of quarters and their attending to complaints. It is not a question 
of contract labour. It is a question of lakhs and lakhs of workers, officers, 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
including MPs, MLAs, dignitaries etc. living in a city like Delhi where there is 
a repeated threat of earthquake. If th ese accommodations are not maintained 
properly and the construction work is not  done properly, it is a threat to their 
life. Even last Tuesday there was an earthquake measuring 5.3 on the richter 
scale. Sir, I had put a question and it has not been answered by the hon. Minister. 
I would like to know how many Government quarters in Delhi are not in a very 
good and habitable condition and whether the Government has decided to 
demolish them and replace them by new construction. What steps is the 
Government taking to repair the quarters and attend to the complaints? 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, in Delhi we receive around 30,000 complaints. 
On an average they come to 2.5 thousand complaints per month. Complaints are 
greater in number during the Monsoon and hot-summer seasons. Last month's 
figures I will supply to the hon. Member. 
We would definitely conduct a survey about all our accommodations to find 
out how many are in dilapidated condition and are not fit for habitation. Sir, there 
is a Budget of Rs. 500 crores for the maintenance of the CPWD quarters and 
offices. It is a huge task. Of course, it should be conducted professionally. The 
CPWD is doing its best, but there is a scope improvement. I solicit the suggestions 
of the hon. Members. 
DR. RAJA RAMANNA: Sir, many of the problems of keeping the Government 
houses in quality conditions are because repairs are started and stopped midway 
and are never, completed I can give you scores of cases where they have come 
to start the work with all the things, maybe even for whitewashing but in the 
processes have destroyed many other things and nothing is done to repair them 
for years. So, the buildings look incomplete and dirty as ever. Of course, for 
senior Officers this is done very fast, but for a large number of houses, they are 
done very carelessly and there is no proper maintenance. They finally say the 
work has been done. If you look at the notebook, it is recorded as work completed, 
whereas actually it has not been completed. I request the Minister to look into 
the "Work-completed Register" as to whether the work has been completed at 
all 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I appreciate the point raised by 
the hon. Member. I am ready to constitute a review committee for looking into 
the working of the CPWD as a whole, about its professionalism and its record in 
clientele satisfaction. It will be done very seen In this connection, I solicit 
valuable suggestions from the Members of this House so that we can implement 
■  * 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
them. We need structural overhauling of the CPWD, to make it more professional, 
more responsive. We are open to suggestions. 
DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Mr. Chairman, Sir, T am thankful to the 
Prime Minister and to the Minister of Urban Development for coming to 
Hyderabad, yesterday, and sanctioning 50,000 houses to the State of Andhra 
Pradesh. In this connection, 1 would lik e to know from the Minister whether 
he has received any complaints from th e beneficiaries, the weaker sections 
for whom these houses are being construc ted, that there are no infrastructure 
facilities available around the housing project. Most of the houses which have 
been constructed are either on the outskirts of the towns or villages. The 
allottees have not occupied these houses so far because the basic amenities 
have not been provided. So, Mr. Chairman, Sir, through you, I request the 
hon. Minister to ensure providing basic amenities like roads, drainage system, 
drinking water facilities and street li ghting. Unless these basic facilities are 
provided, people belonging to the weaker sections will not go and occupy 
those houses. The hon. Minister has just  now informed the House that he is 
going to constitute a review committee for making the CPWD a professional 
organisation. Now, will the Minister consider providing basic infrastructure 
facilities before taking up housing projects for the weaker sections? Our 
colleague, Dr. Dasari Narayana Rao, is not here. His question, Question No. 
182, specifically pertains to the development of towns in Andhra Pradesh. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Mr. Chairman, Sir, there are 3,30,00,000 families 
who are shelterless. Three years back, the NDA Government under the leadership 
of ShriAtal Behari Vajpayeeji, took up this scheme for the first time in the urban 
areas. We are going ahead with the construction of the houses for the poor and 
weaker sections of the society and slum dwellers. Indeed, it is a gigantic task. In 
the last three years, about 36,00000 houses have been constructed. For this 
purpose, land is being provided by the State Government. It is a scheme under 
which land and civic amenities are provided by the respective State Governments; 
and the grant and loan component will be provided by the Union Government. I 
am glad to inform the house that in various States, the scheme has taken off, 
especially, the Valmiki-Ambedkar Awas Yojana. They are doing very well. Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, through you, I would request the hon. Members of this House to 
take up with their State Governments the question of providing land, roads and 
civic amenities under this scheme for the urban poor and slum dwellers forthwith. 
If the Government of Karnataka, the Government of Madhya Pradesh and other 
State Governments come forward with a proposal, we can give Rs. 40,000-

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
Rs. 60,000 as grant, that is, 50 per cent in the form of grant-and 50 per cent loan 
from HUDCO. But they have to provide all the infrastructure facilities so that 
there could be matching grant from the Central Government. 
DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Sir, the Minister should ensure providing of 
infrastructure facilities either by the State Government or by the Central 
Government, before sanctioning a loan. 
Your colleague, Shri Bandaru Dattatraya, who hails from Hyderabad city 
knows about it better than anybody else. Both of us visited many slum areas, 
where there are still unfinished houses. If you verify it from your colleague, you 
will know the actual facts. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: The scheme comes into operation only when 
State Governments come out with a DPR, with a proposal, with all the requisite 
plan, lay-out plan and service plan. Without a lay-out plan or a service plan, the 
scheme cannot be implemented for the development of a locality. Secondly, the 
State Government also gives us a guarantee for the loan, and it also gives us a 
guarantee. "We are providing all these titles to the squatters in the slum areas." 
DR. Y. LAKSHMI PRASAD: Sir, the hon. Minister can inform the House as to 
which State Governments are not coming forth. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, the supplementary does not relate to the main 
question. Despite that, I am answering this question. (Interruptions). I hope, 
hon. Dr. Alladi Rajkumargaru is not complaining about the Andhra Pradesh 
Government. (Interruptions). 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Miss Mabel Rebello. 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: Sir, the maintenance of lifts in Delhi, specially 
where we are staying, is given to priv ate contractors. The private contractor 
engages contract labour and he is making them work for 12 hours and pays them 
Rs. 2000/- each whereas the CPWD, I am told by reliable sources, pays Rs. 5000/ 
- each in respect of these liftmen. Actually, for 12 hours, the contractor gets Rs. 
7,500/- per liftman whereas he pays the liftman only Rs. 2000/-. Thus, there is 
terrible exploitation; and because of that, these liftmen are never available in the 
lifts and we cannot even pull them up. What does the hon. Minister intend to do 
in this regard? There is so much of exploitation in this sector. 
SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: Sir, I request the hon. Member to give me a 
complaint so that I can take immediate action on it. 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: Sir, why should I give a complaint in writing? I am 
saying it here in Parliament. You can take cognizance of that and act on it.

SHRI ANANTH KUMAR: We are not here to support any type of

SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, in connection

†* 184. DR. A. K. PATEL: Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE AMD COMPANY 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of undertrial prisoners for whom hearing has been held till 
October, 2001, after the orders for setting up of special courts in jails passed by

(b) the details thereof State-wise; and 
(c) whether Government propose to put more efforts in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
ARUN JAITLEY): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The Hon'ble Chief Justice of India, on administrative side, wrote a 
letter dated 29th November, 1999 to all the Chief Justice of the High Courts 
suggesting that every Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the Chief Judicial 
Magistrate of the area, in which a District jail falls, may hold his Court once or 
twice in a month, in jail to take up the cases of those under- trial prisioners who

details of number of cases disposed of, State & UT wise, are at Statement-I (See 
below).

followed up by the Registry of the Supreme Court.

DR. A. K. PATEL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is a well-known dictum of the Judiciary 
that justice delayed is justice denied. Today, a number of cases all over the 
country in all the courts, particularly, the trial courts, are pending since long. I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister the number of cases charge-sheeted  
and lying pending for trial, State-wise. 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, in the course of oral reply, I may not be able to give 
the list of cases which are pending in each State. But approximately, the number 
of cases now pending all over the country in the trial courts is about two crores. 
It is about a lakh or so more than two crores, and two-thirds of them, about one 
crore and thirty-four lakhs are criminal cases. I can send to the hon. Member the 
State-wise break-up, if he so desires. 
DR. A. K. PATEL: Sir, the Government of India had just to dispose of the 
cases, and set up Fast Track Courts, About 1734 courts are sanctioned. May I 
know from the hon. Minister the number of courts started all over the country? 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, the Finance Commission had made a 
recommendation pursuant to which the Union Government had requested the 
State Government and the High Courts to set up these courts, preferably five in 
every district, and out of the 173' "ourts which are targeted, 862 courts have 
been notified till date. 
SHRI HANSRAJ BHARDWAJ: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the crux of this question 
is the presence of a large number of under-trials in the Indian jails, and that 
12 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
being so, the Supreme Court has issued directions to speed up the trial of these 
cases by giving special courts. This question of under-trials is a very, very 
important question, and the presence of under-trial is so much that it has raised 
a question mark against our Justice System, particularly, the Criminal justice 
System. I remember in 80's. the old Bhagalpur blinding case, and the presence 
of under-trials in Bihar. This question actually does not relate to the Ministry of 
Law and Justice. It must be answered by the Home Ministry. This has become a 
human rights problem. If a person remains in jail for a year, his whole family 
suffers during his absence if he does not get bail. I would like to draw your 
attention to the problems in jails. I had a brief survey made of the Indian jails 
recently. In Chennai, there was a lathi-ch arge in the jail twice during the last 
year. In Pune, there are five times more prisoners than the jail can accommodate. 
There is no segregation of prisoners in jail. Women and children are made to 
live in these jails. This is a serious human problem, and through the hon. Law 
Minister, I would like to draw the attention of the Home Ministry to this problem. 
I would particularly like to know as to what they are doing to improve the 
conditions in jails, and then to provide a speedy mechanism to ensure that a 
person is not made to live for a longer period than what his actual sentence is. 
Therefore, this needs to be examined  pointedly with respect to the human 
rights problem. May I therefore know from the hon. Law Minister whether he 
agrees with me on this point that this  question needs to be addressed to the 
Home Ministry in greater detail, rather than saying that we are appointing ten 
courts here or twenty courts there und er this provision? This is pointedly a 
malady which faces our justice System. 
Therefore, I want an assurance from the Government that the Government 
will attend to this problem as a human problem. 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, I am very grateful to the hon. Member for having 
raised a very important issue. Particularly, in so far as it relates to undertrials, 
the problem becomes very acute. It is ironical that the percentage of undertrials 
in India is 73 per cent of our total jail population. So, the number of people who 
have still not been tried and convicted is overwhelmingly larger than those 
who are convicted and are still in jails. The hon. Members is right; the Home 
Ministry deals with this issue. I will certainly bring it to their notice because 
the State Governments also have to be invovled. Within these parameters of 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
undertrails, there are also undertrials who are petty offenders; there are undertrials 
who have already*undergone a jail sentence even with or without being 
imprisoned for a reasonably long period of time; there are first-time offenders 
who are also entitled to benefits under the provisions of the Offenders Act, and 
there are several poor undertrials who are unable to afford lawyers or are unable 
to go out on bail because of absence of surety. Now, these are all problems of 
undertrials in a number of cases which are there, and therefore, this experiment 
of judges, going to jail and, therefore,  making an assessment in jail itself, 
holding trials in hundreds of cases, or judges disposing of cases in jails, keeping 
all these factors in mind, with or without trials being held, is an experiment 
which, pursuant to the Supreme Court's request, several State Governments 
have implemented—we have given the figures—and this has been reasonably 
successful in a number of States. Wherever judges have gone to, once or twice 
in a months, the judges have been able to spot out a number of cases, in fact 
hundreds literally, every day, where persons of these categories who need not 
be indefinitely m jail because of want of  a formal trial, have been released. 1 
will certainly bring these facts, and also the issue which the hon. Member has 
raised to the notice of the hon. Home Minister. 
SHRI KULDIP NAYYAR: Has he worked out how long an undertrial stays in 
jail? I mean, for how much period. Has it ever been assessed? 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, to give a definitive period for each and every 
undertrial, it would be difficult. There may be cases where undertrials are also 
well supported, and they are eligible to apply for bail, but courts deny them bail 
because the offence itself is heinous. In these cases, the undertrials have to stay 
in prison for the entire duration of the trial, and the judge decides whether he is 
to be convicted or acquitted. But there are also a large number of cases, which 
I mentioned in the first category—petty offenders, first-time offenders, small 
offences—where undertrials are in jail not because the offence itself is very 
serious and they are unable to come out  on bail, but also because of various 
social circumstances, inability to organise a surety for themselves. I don't think 
we are having across the country any un iform period for this category of 
undertrails. 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: Sir, the Mi nister has stated the reasons for 
pendency, but I think, one main reason is not included in that. Sir, as far as we 
know, in several courts, a large number of posts are lying vacant for long; they 
are not being filled up. This is also one of the main reasons for pendency of the 
cases. I would like to know whether the Government or the Ministry would 
take urgent steps to fill up all the vacancies within a short period of time. 
14 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, mis part of the question relates to vacancies. I may 
inform the hon. Member that this is a problem with regard to which we have been 
regularly addressing the High Courts and the State Governments. The 
recommendations, both in the higher judiciary, i.e. the High Courts, and in the 
subordinate judiciary, are to be initiated by the High Court itself. In the case of the 
High Courts, it is finally notified by the Central Government, and in the case of the 
Subordinate Courts, finally notified by the State Government. The Governor makes 
it on the recommendation of the judiciary itself. As far as the High Courts are 
concerned, we have about 170 vacancies—I have mentioned a similar figure many 
times in the past also—and we have been endeavouring that the High Courts at least 
take effective steps to initiate the process for a large number of these 170 vacancies; 
for almost over a hundred of them, we do not even have, first, the recommendation. 
The Chief Justice of India has always been writing to the Chief Justices of the 
High Courts to expedite, atleast, the initial recommendation. Similarly, as far as 
subordinate courts are concerned, the number of vacancies are, approximately 
1,900, against the total strength of 12,500. Even in this matter, we have been 
writing to the Chief Justices and the State Governments to expedite the 
appointment process. 
PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Hon. Chairman, Sir, in this context, I 
remember what Justice Ratnavel Pandian had remarked in the court itself. He 
said, "the undertrials are suffering much. Hence, I am directing the High 
Courts and the State Governments; if th ey find that the delay is due to the 
Government Pleader or want of Judges, once the time is given, if it exceeds 
more than six months, all the undertrials are to be acquitted." If I remember 
correctly, he made a pronouncement to that effect in the Supreme Court. Has 
the Government got any idea about this? Has the Gove rnment reacted to this 
matter? 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, the Supreme Court had, in the past, on several 
occasions—once in relation to the undertrials In Bihar, and, again, in relation to 
the undertrials across the country—direct ed the release of those undertrials 
who had spent more than a particular period in jails. Those judgements are to be 
implemented by the concerned Subordinate Judges and the State Governments 
and, wherever those directions have been passed, they have been implemented. 
SHRI BACHANILEKHRAJ: Sir, this is a question regarding the undertrial 
prisoners. I would like to know how many cases of undertrial prisoners are 
pending and how many undertrial prisoners are involved in those cases. We 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
are given a reply regarding petty offences. But there are so many cases 
pending in the Sessions Courts. The question is regarding the number of 
undertrial prisoners. That question has not been replied to. The hon. Minister 
may give the number of undertrial prisoners in jails. 
Secondly, there is a practice whereby the cases of undertrials in prisons are 
being conducted on a priority basis. If they are in jails for more than six months, 
it is the duty of the court to take up first the cases of the undertrial prisoners. 
So, I would like to know whether the Minister will be pleased to move the 
courts, through the Supreme Court, and see that the cases of undertrials are 
taken up in preference to other cases so that justice is given to these 
undertrials in time. 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, there were several kinds of figures that the 
hon. Member has suggested. In fact, in every criminal case, whether a person is 
on bail or not, he is an undertrial. I have mentioned the number of cases. The 
total number of criminal cases that I have mentioned is 1,34,00,000. As far as 
the number of undertrial prisoners is concerned—those who are still not being 
convicted but are in jails—it is 1,88,341, according to the last figures received by 
us.

cases. My second suggestion is that these trials should be speeded up so that 
they can be concluded well before 15 years.

Monitoring of AJDs/HIV 
*186.   SHRIC/RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
             SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) how Government monitor the functioning of NGOs working on AIDS/ 
   HIV; and 
(b) the steps taken to curb the menace of AIDS spreading at alarming speed 
in Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) The National AIDS Control Programme-II envisages NGOs as 
critical partners for targeted interventions, voluntary testing and counselling 
and school AIDS education activities. The NGOs are selected by the State AIDS 
Control Societies (SACSs) through a stringent and transparent process. National 
AIDS Control Organization (NACO) has given detailed guidelines for selection, 
capacity building and monitoring of NGOs by the State Societies. 
A detailed monitoring and evaluation system has been built into the process 
of implementation. Regular visits are made by the NGO Adviser and other 
officers of the SACS. The NGOs are required to submit detailed activity reports 
and audited statements of expenditure. The accounts of the NGOs funded are 
also subject to audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General from time to time. 
The State Societies are also required to carry out evaluation of the impact of the 
intervention programmes, through independent agencies. 
(b) The National AIDS Control Programme is a 100% centrally sponsored 
scheme implemented in all States/Union Territories including Andhra Pradesh 
and Maharashtra. The main components consist of: 
—  Reducing the spread of HIV in groups at high risk by identification 
of target populations and providing peer counselling, condom 
promotion and treatment of sexually transmitted infections. 
—  Preventive intervention for the general population by Information, 
Education and Communication (IEC) and awareness campaigns, 
provision of voluntary testing and counselling, safe blood transfusion 
Services and prevention of occupational exposure. 
—  Providing financial assistance for treatment of opportunistic infections, 
home-and community based care. 
—  Strengthening effectiveness and technical, managerial, financial 
32 

[3 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
sustainability of the programme at National, State and Municipal levels. 
—  Promoting collaboration amongst public, private and voluntary sector. 
The Annual Action Plan for 2001-2002 approved for the States of Andhra 
Pradesh and Maharashtra is Rs. 11.06 crores and Rs. 16.84 crores respectively. 
Besides, the approved Action Plan, the bilateral agencies are extending technical 
and financial support for implementation of projects in the States of Andhra 
Pradesh and Maharashtra. 
In the State of Maharashtra, project AVERT funded by United States Agenecy 
for International Development (USAID) has been approved with the objective 
of strengthening the national response to reduce transmission of STD/HIV/ 
AIDS and related infectious diseases. The outlay for the current year is Rs. 7.00 
crores. 
Department for International Development (DFID), UK, is providing financial 
assistance for implementation of the "Partnership for Sexual Health' project for 
the prevention and control of HIV/AIDS and other sexually transmitted infections 
in Andhra Pradesh for a period of five years. The current year's outlay is Rs. 7.00 
crores.

Bidding Discontent 
* 189. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: Will the Minister of DISINVESTMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Govenmenfs attention has been drawn to the news-item captioned 
"Bidding Discontent" which appreared in the Outlook, dated 19th November, 
2001; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps taken, so far, to make the valuation process transparent and 
acceptable within Government's own agencies? 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) 
The disinvestment in Central Public Sector Undertakings is carried out through 
the process of Inter- Ministerial consultations and normally an Inter-Ministerial 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
Group is constituted for each such case . The article which appreared in the 
Outlook dated 19th November 2001 inter alia referred to the views and opinions 
expressed by one of the members of the Inter-Ministerial Group constituted for 
the purpose of disinvestment in IndiaTourism Development Corporation (ITDC). 
The said officer is also one of the members of the Evaluation Committee which 
was constituted for evaluation of the financial bids for disinvestment in ITDC 
Hotels. The suggestions / views expressed have been duly considered. The 
existing procedure involves valuation of the assets of a par ticular enterprise 
under disinvestment by a professional and registered Asset Valuer, selected 
through the process of competitive bidding. The inputs given by the Asset 
Valuer are taken into account by the Advisor to the Government for the 
disinvestment transaction in question. The Advisor is normally a merchant banker 
of repute and selected through the process of open competitive bidding. For 
ensuring uniformity in valuations, the Ministry of Disinvestment has laid down 
guidelines indicating the standard methodologies to be adopted. Such a 
professional skill and experience as available to a reputed merchant banker is 
not normally available in the Government set-up. The Advisors make a 
presentation before the Evaluation Committee and explain the various 
assumptions used in different methodologies. The members of the Evaluation 
Committee deliberate on all the issues and seek clarifications from the Advisors 
on various points. The process of deliberation and consultaiton among the 
members of the Committee goes on for hours together. After the Committee is 
satisfied, it takes a decision about the reserve price suggested by the Advisors. 
The Committee is free to make changes, wherever required. Thereafter the report 
of the Evaluation Committee is placed before an Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) 
for consideration. The recommendations  of the IMG are placed before the 
concerned group of Secretaries for their recommendations and placement of the 
matter before the appropriate final d ecision making authority. The existing 
procedure and methodology was followed in the cases of disinvestment in 
Modem Food Industries Limited (MFIL), Bharat Aluminium Company Limited 
(BALCO) and also in the recently completed disinvestment in CMC Limited 
and HTL Limited. The procedure followe d in the case of MFIL has already 
been seen and scrutinized by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India 
(C&AG). Other cases of disinvestment are also in the process of scrutiny by the 
C&AG of India. The experience gained thus far does not suggest that the existing 
procedure and methodologies need to be modified.

(b) and (c) The existing health infrast ructure is capable of meeting the 
anticipated threat. The Government has taken following actions in the context 
of the present international scenario: 
1.  A detailed list of biological agents used as weapons prepared by the

likely method of dissemination, incubation period, lethality and the 
availability of vaccines, anti-micr obial threapy and treatment has 
been circulated to Health Secretary and Director of Health Services of

 Earmarking of maximum number of beds for emergency contingency.

Delhi-110054, an Institute under Directorate General of Health Services

Confirmation Tests for HIV 
*199. SHRI ANANTRAY DEVSHANKER DAVE: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) which are the tests required to be conduced for confirmation of HIV; 
(b) whether tests for HIV confirmation are different for children less than, 
two years; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether HIV testing machines are available in the Medical Colleges; 
 
58 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) whether these Colleges are authorised to announce the status of an AIDS 
victim; and 
(f) if so, the number of cases detected till date? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) There are various tests available for confirmation of HIV based on 
the detection of antibodies and virus particles. These tests are : (I) Enzyme Linked 
Immunosorbent Assays [ELISA]; (2) Rapid HIV tests; (3) Western Blot [WB]; (4) 
Indirect fluorescent antibody test [IFA]; and (5) Polymerase Chain Reaction 
[PCR] for detecting virus particles. 
Under the National AIDS Control Programme, ELISA and Rapid HIV Assays are 
being used for diagnosis of HIV infected persons, asymptomatic HIV persons and 
epidemiological surveillance. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The HIV status of children below the age of 2 years can be 
detected by a test known as Polymerase Chain reaction. Children have passive 
antibodies from HIV infected mothers which may not reveal the true HIV status of 
the child. These antibodies disappear around 18 months of age when sero 
conversion takes place. Thereafter, HIV can be detected by conventional tests. 
(d) to (f) Yes, Sir. In children below 18 months of age, it is advised to conduct 
PCR test to detect the HIV particles. HIV testing machines, for detecting 
antibodies i.e. ELISA readers are available in a majority of Public Sector Medical 
Colleges; the machines for conducting the polymerase Chain Reaction [PCR] test 
are available at a few centers only, and are not recommended for routine diagnostic 
use. The Medical Colleges are authorized to reveal the status to the HIV/AIDS 
victim only, after pre and post test counseling, and maintaining full confidentiality. 
The cumulative number of AIDS cases, including children, reported till 31st 
October, 2001 is 29007.

international scenario; 
1. A detailed list of biological agents used as weapons prepared by the 
Indian Council of Medical Research along with signs and symptoms, 
likely method of dissemination, incubation period, lethality and the 
availability of vaccines, anti-microbial therapy and treatment has been 
circulated to Health Secretary and Di rector of Health Services of all 
States/UTs., and Central Govt, hospitals advising them to take 
following precautionary steps. 
* Earmarking of maximum number of beds for emergency contingency 
* Stocking of vaccines/sera/drugs to the extent possible. 
* Setting up a special team of doctors for coordinated action. They should 
be sensitized on the impact of such weapons and treatment measures.

Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to review the management 
(diagnosis, treatment, IEC activities etc.) of recently emerging diseases 
of public health importance like Dengue, Anthrax etc. Eminent experts 
in the field of medical science from different organizations in the 
country, senior officials of Ministry of Health & F.W., and chiefs of 
different Government and private hospitals in Delhi participated in the 
meeting and deliberated on various aspects of the bio-terrorism in the 
backdrop of the current global situation. 
3. Two expert group meetings (18th and 21 st October, 2001) were held to 
finalise guidelines to be issued in CD Alert. 
4. National Institute of Communicable Diseases, 22, Sham Nath Marg, 
Delhi-110054, an Institute under Directorate General of Health Services 
has been designated as the nodal ag ency for carrying out the tests of 
suspected Anthrax samples. Around the clock control room is 
functioning Telephone Nos. 3912901 (Between 10.00 A.M. to 6.00 P.M.) 
& 3971875 (Between 6.00 P.M. to 10.00 A.M.) to receive and test the 
suspected samples. Till the evening of 27th November, 2001, 322 
suspected envelopes were received in the NICD for testing. 303 samples 
have already been tested, none was found positive. 
5. CD Alert, a monthly Newsletter of National Institute of Communicable 
Diseases titled "Bioterrorism-Public Health system to Remain Alert" 
exclusively on Anthrax has been wide ly circulated. It has also been 
put in the Website of MOHFW (http:/mohfw.nic.in) for information 
of general public. 
6. Do's & Don'ts has already been published in the leading National Dailies 
regarding Anthrax. 
7. A meeting-cum workshop on Biological & Chemical Terrorism was 
convened by the Department of Health on 29th October, 2001 in New 
Delhi wherein Health Secretary, Home Secretary and Director of Health 
Services from various States/UTs., eminent experts in the field of 
medical science from different organizations in the country and heads 
of different hospitals in Govt, and private sector in Delhi participated 
and deliberated on various aspects. The representatives from the States 
informed the preparatory measures taken by them and assured 
availability of drugs in adequate quantity to tackle any situation.

Increase in Mosquitoes 
† 1411. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMJLY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that mosquitoes causing dengue and malaria 
are increasing; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to restart spraying of DDT under National 
Malaria Eradication Programme in view of ineffectiveness of other measures 
adopted by it; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, in what manner these mosquitoes would be brought under control? 
THE MINISTEROF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): (a) Aedes 
Aegypt mosquito causing Dengue is widespread in different parts of the country, 
specially in urban areas. Its density increase in conducive and favourable conditions. 
Density of the Anopheline mosquito, transmitting malaria, increase during the Monsoon 
or the post-Monsoon season. 
(b) to (d) For controlling malaria DDT continues to be used under national Anti 
Malaria Programme wherever effective and vectors susceptible to this insecticide.

Steps taken for control of Malaria and dengue include :— 
MALARIA 
Early case detection and prompt treatment 
Selective Vector Control 
Promotion of personal protection methods 
Early detection and containment of epidemics 
Information, Education and Co mmunication towards personal 
prevention and community participation 
Institutional and Management Capacity Building, Trained Manpower 
Development and efficient Management Information System (MIS) 
Issuance of advance warning to States / UTs suggesting all the 
preventive and control measures 
DENGUE 
Disease and vector surveillance 
Vector control mainly through source reduction 
Early diagnosis and case management in hospitals 
Information, Education and Communication for community awareness 
Early response to epidemics 
Regular monitoring and review of Dengue situation by the concerned 
authorities

dropouts at primary and secondary school levels to below 20 percent for

1423. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have stopped the practice of setting targets for 
important family welfare programmes; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) how Government propose to improve performance of family welfare 
programmes, especially in BIMARU States? 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001 ] 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. THAKUR): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Upto 31st March, 1996, the achievements of Family Welfare Programme 
were assessed on the basis of the targets given from above for individual 
contraceptives. This led to a situation where the achievements of contraceptives 
targets had become ends in themselves. This target, system was started with the 
concepts that the achievement of contraceptive target would definitely lead to 
decrease in birth rate and subsequently in decrease in population. However, over 
the years it was realized that in the target system there were many drawbacks. 
For instance, users preference in choosing contraceptive was not reflected: due 
to non-availability of required contracep tives for the users, targets were not 
realized; there was no system of feed back on contraceptives needs- of users and 
thus the quality of services to the beneficiaries did not receive due attention. 
(c) Currently, six Area Projects are bein g implemented in the selected 
Districts/Cities of 13 States including Delhi at a total cost of Rs. 1194.78 crores 
with the financial assistance from World Bank, DANIDA, DFID (UK), UNFPA 
and German Government. In addition, under the World Bank Assisted RCH 
programme, 24 RCH Sub-project (17 Districts and 7 Cities) are under 
implementation in 17 States at a total co st of Rs. 283.88 crores for a period of 
five years since October, 1997. 
The National Population Policy, 2000 adopted by the Government in 
February, 2000 envisages strengthening and energizing the Family Welfare 
services in the four States of Bihar, M.P., Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh including 
all other States. 
An Empowered Action Group has been constituted within the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare, for preparing area specific programmes with special

1426.     SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN: 
     SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA:  
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the recent trials on human subjects of 
an anti-cancer drug in Regional Cancer Centre at Thiruvananthapuram without 
following the rules properly; 
(b) if so, whether any probe has been conducted into the incident; 
(c) if so, the outcome of the same; 
(d) whether Government propose to give interim relief to the victims; if 
not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether Government propose to issue certain ethical guidelines on bio-
medical research to avoid such incidents in future; 
(f) if so, the details thereof; and 
(g) the fresh steps taken to make rule s relating to clearance for clinical 
trials more stringent? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR):(a)Yes,sir. 
(b) to (d) A team constituted by the Central Government has investigated the 
alleged use of banned drug on cancer patients at Regional Cancer Centre, 
Thiruvananthapuram. The Central team observed that though violation of human 
rights or use of banned drug was not involved in the trial, however, there have 
been lapses in respect of the regulatory procedure required to be followed for 
conducting such trials in the country. 
Regional Cancer Centre, Thiruvananthapuram has been served a show cause 
notice and advised to suspend all ongoing clinical trials with drugs for a period of six 
months. They have also been advised to obtain all necessary approvals from the 
government and revise the list of ethical committee members of the centre. 
In view of above, the question of giving interim relief does not arise. 
(e) and (f) Indian Council of Medi cal Research (ICMR), New Delhi has 
published "Ethical Guidelines for Bio-medical Research on human Subject" which 
will be followed by all researchers/institutions engaged in bio-medical research 
in the country.

Casualties due to overdose of Vitamin-A in Nagaon District 
1428. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the casualties due to overdose of Vitamin-A in Nagaon 
district of Assam on 12th November, 2001 during administration of UNICEF 
sponsored vaccine as well as food poisoning cases due to intake of pulses in 
various parts of Assam during the last six months; and 
(b) the lives lost and suffered, causes detected and responsibilities fixed for 
such incidents alongwith date and location-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) and (b) As per information furnished by the State Government 
of Assam after the recent Vitamin A ca mpaign 689 children were treated for 
minor illnesses without hospitalization; 41 were hospitalized and released after 
recovery; and 5 children are redported to have died in Nagaon district. Four 
out of the five children who died did not receive Vitamin A. The remaining 
child was suffering from fever for one week prior to death. 
After consuming soaked gram on 10th August 2001 after a peace rally held 
the day earlier, 1819 children suffered from diarrhoea and vomiting in Barpeta 
district. Of these two died. 230 students and 44 members of the staff suffered 
from food poisoning in Assam Valley School in Sonitpur district on 7.9.2001. 
470 people attending the Flag Hoisting ceremony at Banbari Mini Stadium in 
Nalbari district on 15th August 2001 suffered food poisoning on 16th August 
2001. One death is reported. 60 cases of food poisoning were reported from 
village Niz-Sipajhar in Darrang district after consuming Prasad of 'Matimah' on 
17.9.2001. Kamrup district reported 11 cases of food poisoning from Rangia. In 
the same district 17 students of Kachari Basti School, Guwahati suffered food 
poisoning on 5.9.2001. 
The State Government has collected samples of pulses and water from the 
affected districts. Some samples of pulses were found to contain 
organophosphorus and some samples of water were found to be contaminated 
with coliform organisms. Free medical treatment was provided to the affected 
people. Bakeries have been instructed to sell fresh and quality products only. 
The district authorities stopped sale of moog, gram etc., People were advised 
not to consume grams, moogs and their products by circulating leaflets, through 
newspapers and other media.

1446. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state as in the case of Legislative and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

Executive, whether Government have worked out some mechanism or arrangement 
like Lokpal to work as code of conduct for the Judges so that the members of the 
Judiciary are subject to disciplinary and Conduct Rules framed by the State 
Governments and the High Courts? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
ARUN JAITLEY): The issue of Judicial  Accountability was discussed at the 
Conference of Chief Justices held in 1990 and on the basis of the broad consensus 
emerging out of the deliberations, the Chief Justice of India summed up the 
position as follows: 
"The Chief Justice "Of the High Court has the competence to receive 
complaints against the conduct of the Judges of his court and when 
he receives any he would look into it for finding out if it deserves to 
be closely looked into. Where he is satisfied that the matter requires 
to be examined, he shall have f acts ascertained in such manner as 
he considers appropriate keeping the nature of allegations in view 
and if he is of the opinion that the matter is such that it.should be 
reported to the Chief Justice of India, he shall do so. 
The Chief Justice of India shall act in a similar manner in regard to 
complaints relating to conduct of Judges of the Supreme Court and 
in regard to conduct of Chief Justices of the High Courts. 
On the basis of the facts ascertain ed, the Chief Justice of the High 
Court or the Supreme Court, as the case may be shall take such 
appropriate action as may be considered proper, keeping the interests 
of the judiciary as the paramount consideration." 
The complaints received against the Judges of the Supreme Court and the 
High Courts are dealt with in the manner indicated above. 
One of the items of the National Agenda for Governance is to set up a 
National Judicial Commission (NJC) to make recommendations for judicial 
appointment in the Supreme Court of India and the High Courts and to draw up 
a Code of Ethics. The Government is committed to the idea of setting up the 
Commission to deal with these matters. 
The subject matter regarding corruption in lower Judiciary is the concern of 
the respective High Court in accordance wi th the provisions of article 235 of 
the Constitution of India.

1470. iClISS. MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND

wise; and 
(c) how do Government ensure compliance of these rules by State

THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JU STICE AND EMPOWERMENT (DR. 
SATYANARAYAN JATIYA): (a) The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes 
(Prevention of Atrocities) Rules, 1995 were notified vide No. 145 dated 31.03.1995. 
Rule 3 of the said Rules provide for precautionary and preventive measures which 
provide that the State Government shall take the following measures with a view 
to prevent atrocities on Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes:— 
(i) Identify the area where it has reasons to believe that atrocity may 
take place or there is an apprehension of recurrence of an offence 
under the Act; (ii) Order the District Magistrate and Superintendent 
of Police or any 
other to visit the identified area and review the law and order 
situation; (Hi) If deem necessary, in the identified area, cancel the arms 
licenses of the 
persons, not being members of the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled 
Tribes, their near relations, servants or employees and family friends and 
get such arms deposited in the Government Armoury; (iv) Seize all 
illegal fire arms and prohibit any illegal manufacture of 
fire arms; (v) With a view to ensure the safety of person and 
property, if deem 
necessary, provide arms licenses to the members of the Scheduled 
Castes and the Scheduled Tribes; (vi) Constitute a high power State-
level committee, district and divisional 
level committees or such number of other committees as deem proper 
and necessary for assisting the Government in implementation of 
the provisions of the Act; (vii) Set-up a vigilance and monitoring 
committee to suggest effective 
measures to implement the provisions of the Act; 
190 

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(viii) Set-up Awareness Centres and organize Workshops in the identified 
area or at some other place to educate the persons belonging to the 
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes about their rights and 
the protection available to them under the provisions of various Central 
and State enactments or rules, regulations and schemes framed 
thereunder; 
(ix) Encourage Non-Government Organizations for establishing and 
maintaining Awareness Centre and organizing Workshops and 
provide them necessary financial and other sort of assistance; 
(x) Deploy special police force in the identified area; 
(xi) By the end of every quarter, review the law and order situation, 
functioning of different committees, performance of Special Public 
Prosecutors, Investigating Officers and other Officers responsible 
for implementing the provisions of the Act and the cases registered 
under the Act. 
(b) and (c) The details of various measures taken by the States / UTs as well 
as by the Central Government are contained in the Annual Report which is 
laid on the Table of each House of Parliament by the Central Government, in 
accordance with Section 21 (4) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled 
Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The Annual Report for the year 
ended 31.12.1998 has already been laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha on 
06.08.2001 and the Table ofLok Sabha on 08.08.2001 and the report contains the 
State wise details of measures taken. 
The Central Government is also taking following measures in co-ordination 
with the State Governments / Union Territory Administrations for preventing 
atrocities against SCs / STs:—  
(i) Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for implementation of the 
Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the Scheduled Castes and 
the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, central 
assistance is provided to the State Governments on 50:50 basis and 
to Union Territory Administration on 100% basis, for effective 
implementation of the Acts, which include legal aid, appointment

periodic surveys, identification of atrocity prone areas and providing 
relief and rehabilitation to victims / dependents of atrocity victims.

1989 during last three years as reported by States/UTs are shown in the statement 
{see below). 
(b) The Central Government is taking following measures in co-ordination 
with the State Governments/Union Territory Administrations for preventing 
atrocities against SCs/STs. 
(i) Under the Centrally Sponsored scheme for implementation of the 
Protection of Civil rights Act, 1955 and the Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, central 
assistance is provided to the State Governments on 50:50 basis and 
to union Territory administration of 100% basis, for effective 
implementation of the Act, which include legal aid, appointment of 
officers for initiating or exercising supervision over prosecution, 
setting up of Committees, Special Cells, Special Courts, conducting 
periodic surveys, identification of atrocity prone areas and providing 
relief and rehabilitation to victims/dependents of atrocity victims. 
(ii) State Government, where penden cy of cases is high, have been 
requested to establish exclusive Special Courts for expeditious 
disposal of cases registered. 
(iii) Chief Secretaries of States/UTs have been requested by the Ministry 
of Social Justice & Empowerment for ensuring effective implementation 
of provisions of the Act and policies as also the delivery of services 
and justice to the victims and target group. 
(iv) Chief Ministers of all States/UTs have been requested to take following 
steps:—  
(a) Issuing suitable instructions to the authorities for implementing the Acts 
in letter and spirit. 
(b) Giving particular attention for maintenance of law and order in the identified 
atrocity prone areas.

(c) Taking special measures, as deemed  necessary to protect the life and 
property of Scheduled Castes and Sche duled Tribes in sensitive areas, where 
crime rate is high. 
(d) Ensure speedy disposal of cases file d to provide timely justice to the 
affected persons, filing appeal in time in respect of acquittal cases, based on 
the factual details. 
(e) Involving the elected public representatives and non-governmental 
organizations suitably at State, District, Block and Village level for giving required 
protection to the affected persons and implementation of the Act. 
(f) Training of personnel especially of the police and investigating agencies 
as also in procedures, prosecution etc. 
(v) Implementation of the Act is reviewed in the annual conference of 
the State Secretaries of Scheduled Castes Development and Social 
Welfare Department and the Secretaries are requested to take effective 
measures for implementation of Act. 
(c) The relief to the victims of atrocity, their family members and dependent 
is paid by the State governments/Union Territories Administrations in 
accordance with the "Norms for relief Amount' as prescribed under Rule 12(4) 
of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) 
Rules, 1995. The amount of such relief ranges from Rs. 20,000/- to Rs. 2,00,000/- 
depending upon the offence described in the aforesaid rules. Information on 
relief paid case wise is maintained by the State Governments/Union Territory 
Administrations concerned.

Low literacy pockets in tribal areas of Gujarat 
1482. SHRI AHMED PATEL: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have identified low literacy pockets in tribal areas 
of Gujarat particularly amongst the tribal girls and women; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps Government have taken to spread literacy in such pockets of 
the State? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JUAL ORAM): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The districts having less than 10% literacy rate among ST women as per 
1991 census have been identified as low literacy pockets in the country. Kutch 
and Banaskantha districts in Gujarat have been so identified. 
(c) A new Scheme of Educational Complex in Low Literacy Pockets for 
Development of Women Literacy in Tribal Areas was introduced in 1993-94 to 
spread literacy in the low literacy pockets so identified. Under the Scheme, as 
many as five complexes have so far been set up for educating the tribal girls in the 
identified low literacy pockets of the State of Gujarat

1483. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

under SCA to Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP);

[3 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA

(c) whether Government have conducted any review of the manner of 
utilization of SCA; 
(d) whether Government have deputed any official for the spot verification 
of works; and 
"  (e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JUAL ORAM): (a) and (b) In 
the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the year ended 
March, 1998, it has, inter- alia, been brought out that scrutiny of records in 
selected districts of An dhra Pradesh, Assam, Bi har, Himachal Pradesh, 
Jammu & Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, 
Tripura, West Bengal and Daman & Diu revealed that funds aggregating Rs. 
85.88 crores, which pertain to Special Ce ntral Assistance to Tribal Sub Plan 
were diverted to other schemes/activities. These observations are based on 
sample check of documents for the period 1992-98 of the Ministry and the 
implementing departments and agencies of 17 States and one U.T. The matter 
has been taken up with the State Govts, concerned. 
(c) to (e) Central Government Officer s visit the States/UTs for reviewing 
and ascertaining the progress of implementation of schemes. Meetings/ 
conferences are convened at Central leve l with Ministers in-charge of Tribal 
Welfare of States along with the concerned Secretaries to review physical and 
financial progress of schemes/projects. In addition, the following measures are 
also taken to ensure effective and timely utilization of Central grants under 
SCA: 
(i) Utilisation Certificates are insisted upon as a pre-requisite for further 
release of funds; 
(ii) Periodic progress reports regarding the status of implementation of 
schemes are obtained;

Rate of royalty on Crude Oil 
SHRI ANANTRAY DEVSHANKER DAVE (G ujarat): Sir, the rate of 
royalty on crude oil and gas is being fixed by the Central Government and is 
revised from time to time. Initially, the price of indigenous crude oil and royalty 
was determined by the Administered Pricing Mechanism (APM) system. 
The Government of India has now announced the phase-wise 
dismantling of the APM with effect from 01-04-1998 on petroleum products, 
thereby linking the price of  the indigenous crude with that of the international 
price of comparable crude. In the phase dismantling programme, it has been 
accepted, in principle, to value the crude oil produced indigenously at par with 
the prevailing market price in the inte rnational market for comparable crude. 
The Government of India has cons tituted a Committee, under the 
Chairmanship of Joint Secretary (Exploration), Ministry of Petroleum and 
Natural Gas, New Delhi, to decide the rate of royalty payable to the State 
Governments. At present, the ad hoc rate of royalty on crude oil is Rs. 
850/MT with effect from 1.12.1999. 
The Gujarat Government has made several representations to the 
Government of India to increase the royalty rate on crude oil. The salient 
points are as follows: 
1. The royalty rates for the period 1993 to 1998 should be finalised at 
the earliest. Royalty should be based on the intrinsic value of crude 
oil or international price, whichever is higher. Royalty should be fixed 
at the rate of 40 per cent of the selling price. 
2. The State Government has emphasized that the royalty rate beyond 
1.4.1998 should be linked with the in ternational price of comparable 
crude, and the Government of India' s notification for dismantling the 
regime should be enforced in totality, and the ad hoc fixhq of the 
price of crude oil should be done away with.

the period 1993-98 and the new scheme of royalty from 1.4.1998 onwards, 
the State Government is facing a huge monetary loss. ,

Need to establish an Institute of Seismological   Research in Gujarat 
SHRI GOPALSINH G. SOLANKI (Gujarat ): Sir, Gujarat is a State 
which has experienced two major earthquakes of a magnitude of more than 
8.0 on the Richter Scale, and more than twenty earthquakes of a magnitude of 
more than 5.0 on the Richter Scale, from the year 1819 to 2001. I may also 
state that this year also, the State has experienced more than 250 after-
shocks with a magnitude of 3.8 to 4.9, in the region of Kutch and Saurashtra. 
The earthquake of 26 th January, 2001 was the severest, which had damaged 
property worth about Rs. 50,000 cror es, and had taken 12,000 odd lives. The 
Gujarat region, being on seismic line, coul d face more devastations in future 
also, if earthquakes occur again. It cannot be denied that this is because of the 
increasing population density and levelling up of industrial and civil 
infrastructure. Sir, Gujarat does not have any Seismological Research Institute 
to help in such a situation, and save th e people from _the disaster. Therefore, 
it has become a necessity to establish an  Institute of Seismological Research 
in Gujarat so that lives could be saved by studying the intensity of the coming 
earthquake well in advance, and the people could be informed to take 
precautions, and damages could be prevent ed. This institution will be of great 
importance for collecting data from nearby stations and informing the 
predictions, if any, to the people. Besi des, this institute shall not only be 
teaching short-term courses, but shall also  teach up to the level of graduation, 
post-graduation as well as research studies, to about 140 students for which 
Rs. 26 crores, under non-Plan scheme, and Rs. 7 crores, under Plan scheme, 
shall be required. This may please be sanctioned by the Department of 
Science and Technology. Also, this project be permitted to be implemented, in 
consultation with the network of the overseas institutions.   Therefore, I urge

upon the Government to sanction t he establishment of an Institute of 
Seismological Research in the State of Gujarat, with full financial support from 
the Department of Science and Technology.

Need to develop vaccine for Hepatitis -C 
PROF. M.M. AGARWAL (Uttar Pradesh): Hon'ble Chairman, Sir, 
every fifteenth Indian - that  is, around 12.5 million people of the country- is 
infected by Hepatitis -C. Sir, it is a dreaded disease, as, compared to other 
diseases, its recovery rate is only 50 per cent. It is a silent killer. The Hepatitis 
virus attacks the liver, which is an important organ of the body. Hepatitis leads 
to jaundice, cirrhosis or liver cancer. The Hepatitis virus is transmitted through 
contaminated water, infected injectio n needles, unsafe sex, contaminated 
blood, etc. Despite all these things, no vaccine is yet available for Hepatitis -
C. Safe drinking water has not been provided to the people   of   the   country,   
and   awareness   about   sex   among   masses,

mushrooms, where professionals, like drug addicts, sell their blood.

SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMAD KHAN (DURRU) (Rajasthan): Sir, 
democracy is of the people, for the pe ople and by the people. To ensure that 
each voter can avail of this fundamental right to vote, the Election Commission 
compiles voters' list from time to time and ensures that these votes are cast. 
For this purpose, it takes the help of  the local administration and the State 
Governments. This is the very foun dation of democracy and requires that 
honesty and impartiality be observed. Unfortunately, this sense of honesty has 
been corrupted. An MP from Rampur, Uttar Pradesh, had recently filed a 
complaint with the Central Election Commission about the major discrepancies 
in the electoral rolls in Thakurdwara Assembly constituency. 
Upon scrutiny by the CEC, it was discovered that, indeed, names of 
15,800 people from the minority community were missing from the rolls, and 
21,000 fictitious names of the majori ty community were incorporated. The 
CEC instructed the State Government to  suspend four senior officials and 
transfer 10 others. It is suspected that the ruling party and the Government of 
Uttar Pradesh intend to use the same tactic in the upcoming elections. Several 
parties have expressed their concern over the legality of the electoral rolls in 
the whole of Uttar Pradesh.

carefully scrutinize the electoral lists to avoid any sort of rigging, reinduct the 
names of voters that were deleted, and remove the fictitious names in order to 
have a free and fair election.

THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Sir, I beg to move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Companies Act, 1956, as 
passed by the Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
This amendment to the Companies Act of 1956 is intended to bring 
about a procedural change in the procedure of buy-back of shares by 
companies themselves. 
Sir, in the year 1999, after in itially it was promulgated as an 
Ordinance, the Companies Amendment Ac t of 1999 was passed by this hon. 
House. That Act had added the provis ion of section 77A, and permitted a 
company to buy-back up to 25 per cent of its share capital. Originally, the 
concept of a company was that a company could never be permitted to buy-
back its own shares. But the corporate governance the world over changed, 
and companies were also permitted to buy-back shares, and in 1999, we 
amended our own Companies Act, enabling our companies to also buy-back 
up to 25 per cent of the company shares . After a buy-back is completed, there 
are two processes the world over, either those shares are kept in treasury for 
being redistributed again in future or those shares are destroyed after the buy-
back itself. We had opted to take the se cond option. Sir, this amendment only 
brings about a procedural change. The procedural change being that whereas 
to permit 25 per cent of the buy-back, a Special Resolution of the AGM or the 
EGM of the company is required for purc hasing up to 10 per cent out of those 
25 per cent of the shares, the pr ocedure has been made simpler. For 
purchase of ten per cent of the shares or buy-back of the ten per cent of the 
shares, the Board of Directors of a company is being empowered. Under the 
corporate governance, there are severa l powers which are there with the 
Annual General Body of the company. There are also powers which are there 
with the management of the company. The second change which has been 
brought about is that a company whic h buys-back its shares, cannot buy-back 
a second tranche within 365 days. Therefore, a one year gap would have to be 
maintained, and thirdly, a company for th e next six months is not permitted to 
make any fresh issue of capital of the shares of the company itself. These are 
the three procedural changes, which have been brought. The object of this is 
to simplify the procedure and enable the compalny to buy-back, because a 
suggestion was made as to how does it help small shareholders and the 
investors as far as the company is concerned. Sir, the object of simplifying the 
buy-back procedure up to ten per cent and enabling the companies to buy-
back, particularly, in a situation

THE INDIAN SUCCESSION (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Madam Deputy Chairman, I move : 
"That the Bill further to amend the Indian Succession Act, 
I925,be taken into consideration." 
The Indian Succession Act, 1925, was aimed at consolidating the law 
relating to testamentary and intestate su ccession, as was prevalent at that 
time in the country. Chapter II of Part V of this Act mainly deals with intestate 
succession of Christians. There are two pa rticular provisions which this Bill 
seeks to amend. Section 32 of the Act, in this Chapter, recognizes 
288 

[3 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
the Christian widow as one of the successors to succeed to the property of her 
deceased husband. However, there is an Ex planation attached to it, the effect 
of the Explanation is, if, at the time of the marriage, there is an agreement 
between the wife and husband, in that event, the wife, on becoming a widow, 
will be excluded from her husband's succession. Madam, though this was 
originally conceived to be something which would have been opposed to 
public policy, because there was a specific statutory provision in 1925, this has 
been sustained. We have been receivi ng various representat ions that this 
should be done away with from the statute book; and such a provision should 
have no recognition, particularly, in the present age. The Kerala Women's 
Commission and several other non-Governmental organisations and various 
Christian Women's organisations have been representing to the Government 
that this Explanation should be deleted and a Christian widow should be 
entitled to succeed to the property of her husband, particularly, if he dies 
intestate. 
The second provision is with regard to the provisions of Section 213 
of the Indian Succession Act. This is in tended to bring the Christians on par 
with other communities in the country. T he provisions of Section 213 does not 
apply to Muslims. It also doesn't apply to Hindus, Jains and Buddhists, except 
a certain category who live in 3 metropolitan towns. Since there is no demand 
yet in relation to that category of the Hindus, we are not looking into those at 
the moment. But, with regard to Christians, an exception has been made that 
upon the death of a Christian, there is  a probate mandatorily required to be 
obtained by his successors all over the country. This is a long-drawn process 
where Christian heirs have to go to court and spend money on litigation and 
then get the order of the court to enabl e them to succeed to the predecessor 
interests. 
Some months ago, I received a representation signed by Christian 
Members of Parliament belonging to both Houses of Parliament. About 23 
Members wanted a change in this particul ar provision. Thereafter, I consulted 
various other Christian organisations and they were" also in favour of the 
change. The Law Commission, in its 110 th Report, the Christian Women's 
Commission, Members of Parliament a nd other community leaders have all 
been requesting us to make a change in  this provision.

just to bring the Indian Christians at  par with the words 'Mohammedans' used 
in section 213 so that they are also not expected to go through this

predecessor-in-interest. 
Since this is a provision which seeks to help the community and also 
delete one provision which is now considered unconscionable with regard to 
excluding a widow from her husband's property, I request the hon. House to 
take it up for consideration and pass it.

SHRI S. NIRAIKULATHAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I rise to speak on the 
National Commission for Safai Karamcharis Amendment Bill, 2001, on behalf 
of AIADMK. 
This Bill seeks to extend the te rm of the present Commission up to 
29,h February, 2004. The National Commission for Safai Karamcharis was 
originally set up in 1994. Even after 8 years, the conditions of safai 
karamcharis have not improved. 
The National Human Rights Commission and the National 
Commission for Safai Karamcharis had decided to eliminate manual 
scavenging several years before. But this practice is still going on. 
Employment of Manual Scavengers and  Construction of Dry Latrines 
(Prohibition) Act was passed in 1993. Yet, it was not implemented 
wholeheartedly. Under the Constitution, every citizen has a right to live with 
dignity.   But these safai karamcharis live in misery and squalor because they

National Scheme of Liberation and Rehabilitation of scavengers and their

that all the class IV workers in the country live with dignity.

The Cine-workers Welfare Fund (Amendment) Bill, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Cine-workers Welfare 
Fund Act, 1981, as passed by the Lok Sabha, be taken into 
consideration." 
As the hon. Members are aware,  the Cine-workers Welfare Fund 
Act,'1981 is a piece of progressive social welfare legislation enacted for the 
benefit of cine - workers. The Act envi sages extension of welfare measures 
such as health, medical care and educational assistance to cine - workers and 
their family members. The corpus of t he Fund is created out of a Cess levied 
and collected as a duty of excise on feature films certified by the Central 
Board of Film Certification, which is credited to the Consolidated Fund of India 
under Section 5 of the Cine-workers Welfare Cess Act, 1981. 
The fund is utilised for financing activities to promote the welfare of 
workers employed in cine industry. Presently, there are approximately 63,000 
cine-workers in the country, out of wh ich only 30,000 workers are getting 
benefits under the ongoing welfare sc hemes. The reason is that the 
wage/remuneration limit prescribed un der the Act has become insignificant 
and a large Viumber of workers remain outside the scope of definition Of cine-
workers due to increase in their wages/remuneration over a period of time. 
The ceiling of Rs.1,600/- p.m., where remuneration is paid by way of 
monthly wages, or a sum of Rs.8,000/- where such remuneration has been by 
way of lump sum, is prescribed under sub-section (b) (ii) of Section 2 for 
making the cine-workers entitled to welfare benefits under the Act. 
321 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2001] 
This ceiling was last revised in 1987 by  an amendment of the Act. Since then 
there has been substantial increase in the wages/remuneration of cine-
workers. But since there has also b een a commensurate increase in prices, 
there has been a continuous demand to  increase the wage/remuneration limit 
under the Act so that the cine work ers, who are presently outside the 
definition of cine-workers due to incr eased wages/remuneration, are also 
covered under the definition of cine-workers for the purpose of the Act. 
In view of the aforesaid facts and in  order to bring the bulk of the 
hitherto uncovered cine-workers under the ambit of the welfare provisions, it is 
proposed to remove the existing ceiling on wages/remuneration given in 
Section 2 (b) (ii) of the Cine-work ers Welfare Fund Act, 1981, and authorise 
the Central Government to prescribe t he wages/remuneration of cine-workers 
by issue of notification in the Gazette of India fr om time to time, by an 
amendment to Section 2 (b) (ii) of the Cine-Workers Welfare Fund Act, 1981, 
so that increase in the ceiling of remuner ation of cine-workers, in case it is 
considered necessary and desirable, can be notified from time to time without 
amending the Act frequently. 
By this amendment, more cine-workers would be added thus raising 
the total number of cine-workers to be covered under the welfare provisions. 
With these words, I commend the Bill for the unanimous support of 
the august House. 
The Question was proposed.

o'clock; sometimes, it goes up to the night. All that time, the workers are fully 
engaged in their work. For attending the work, they have to come by four or 
five in the morning. It means, in a day, on an average, they work for 12 to 14 
hours. There is no labour machinery to see whether the labour laws regarding 
working hours are being pr operly implemented or not. There is no weekly off; 
there is no bonus; there is no gratuity  to these workers. These workers are not 
covered under the provident fund scheme. So, these are the poor conditions in 
which these people are working. The film industry is spread over Maharashtra, 
Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Karnataka, Gujarat, Orissa and 
Kerala. Now, out of 63,000 workers that  are listed, hardly 30,000 workers and 
their dependents are getting the benefits under the existing scheme. According 
to the amendment, the Government, by no tification, can fix the income limits 
for eligibility for enrolment in the scheme. It is right. It should be enhanced, but 
there should be a provision for periodica l revision of the eligibility criterion; 
otherwise, it will not be beneficial to t he workers. The cost of living is rising 
day-by-day. I suggest that there should be a machinery for doing periodical 
revision of this scheme. If they add 33,000 new workers to this scheme, 
wherefrom will the money come? The income, as estimated, is Rs.50 lakhs. 
The calculation is that if all these 63, 000 workers are enrolled in the scheme, 
then there would be an expenditure of Rs.45 lakhs, which means, no 
enhancement in the benefits is visualised. That is the point. Sir, I have already 
mentioned about the poor conditions in  which these workers are Iving. The 
Government should increase their educational, hospitalisation and other 
benefits. The Government should also tr y to cover a wider section of workers 
under it. The money should come from th e industry itself so that the coverage 
would be more. Now, the provision is that  the collection will be made only from 
the film producers who produce at least five films. It should be brought down to 
at least three. Not only that; the film industry is
